indicator_names: Grade 3 state English language arts test, percent proficient or advanced; Grades 3-8 state English language arts test, percent proficient or advanced
pathway: Tutoring programs that build children's reading skills raise scores on standardized reading tests, the skill the state English language arts test measures.
evidence_tier: A for the tutoring model only
conditions: Tutoring by trained teachers or paraprofessionals, during the school day, at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or in small groups; volunteer tutoring counts only with a smaller expected gain; plan on the at-scale size, not the pooled size.
typical_effect: Pooled gain of 0.29 standard deviations on literacy tests across randomized trials (0.37 for all outcomes in the 2020 working paper); large United States programs (1,000 or more students) about 0.16 standard deviations; volunteer reading tutoring trials 0.10 (Reading Partners) and 0.13 (Experience Corps) standard deviations on reading comprehension. Plan on the at-scale 0.16 standard deviations, not the pooled size.
key_studies: Nickow, A., Oreopoulos, P., & Quan, V. (2020). The Impressive Effects of Tutoring on PreK-12 Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence. NBER Working Paper 27476. Published as Nickow, Oreopoulos & Quan (2024), The Promise of Tutoring for PreK-12 Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence, American Educational Research Journal, doi:10.3102/00028312231208687 | Kraft, M. A., Schueler, B. E., & Falken, G. T. (2024). What Impacts Should We Expect from Tutoring at Scale? Exploring Meta-Analytic Generalizability. EdWorkingPaper No. 24-1031, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://doi.org/10.26300/zygj-m525 | Jacob, R. T., Armstrong, C., & Willard, J. A. (2015, March). Mobilizing Volunteer Tutors to Improve Student Literacy: Implementation, Impacts, and Costs of the Reading Partners Program. New York: MDRC. (Earlier brief: Jacob, R. T., Smith, T. J., Willard, J. A., & Rifkin, R. E., June 2014, "Reading Partners: The Implementation and Effectiveness of a One-on-One Tutoring Program Delivered by Community Volunteers," MDRC Policy Brief.) | Morrow-Howell, N., Jonson-Reid, M., McCrary, S., Lee, Y., & Spitznagel, E. (2009). Evaluation of Experience Corps: Student reading outcomes (CSD Research Report 09-01). St. Louis: Washington University, Center for Social Development. Reviewed in WWC Quick Review, February 2010.
excerpts: We find that tutoring programs yield consistently substantial positive impacts on learning, with an overall pooled ES of 0.288 SD (SE = 0.029, p < 0.001). ESs tend to be largest for programs that use teachers or paraprofessionals as tutors | We conduct an expanded meta-analysis of 265 randomized controlled trials [...] Pooled effect sizes from studies with stronger target-equivalence remain meaningful but are only a third to a half as large as those from our full sample. | The effect size of each impact, which reflects the magnitude of the difference between the program and control groups, was 0.10 standard deviations for reading comprehension, 0.09 for reading fluency, and 0.11 for sight word efficiency. | Students in the Experience Corps program made greater gains over the academic year on passage comprehension and on general reading skills as assessed by their teachers, with effect sizes of 0.13 and 0.16, respectively.
caveats: Outcomes were study-administered or national standardized reading tests, not the Pennsylvania test. At scale, effects are a third to a half of the full-sample size. Effects were larger for teacher and paraprofessional tutors, earlier grades and school-day delivery, and smaller after school. The scale meta-analysis covers kindergarten to grade 12 in wealthy (OECD) countries, not only the United States. Volunteer programs often assign two or more tutors per child by design. Bounded by the after-school reading null and negative results (structured after-school reading row) and the 21st Century Community Learning Centers null.
model_match_required: Tutoring during the school day by paid, trained tutors (teachers or paraprofessionals), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, with reading as the content. A partner coded Literacy: Reading and Writing (Y1.1) that does not run this model gets no evidence level from this link. Volunteer tutoring counts only at the smaller volunteer-trial size.
magnitude_note: At 0.16 standard deviations, about 6 more participants in 100 reach proficient, assuming participants resemble the District's tested students (base rate about 31 to 33 percent). If the partner tutors 10 percent of a school's tested students, the school rate rises about 0.6 percentage points. Volunteer-trial sizes (0.10 to 0.13) give about 4 to 5 more in 100 participants.
review_verdict: Keep with changes (methods reviewer): tier applies to the model, not to a reading outcome statement; lead with the at-scale 0.16 standard deviations because pooled effects are likely inflated by publication bias; no study used the state test. Applied.
corpus_statements_matching_model: About 29 of 115 statements (about 25 percent; about 17 of 73 organizations) describe tutoring or structured reading help; dose, staffing and timing are almost never stated. 35 statements are a City template line and 31 come from arts, sports and other enrichment.

ESs tend to be largest for programs that use teachers or paraprofessionals as tutors
caveats: One program (Saga) in Chicago; the first trial enrolled boys only. The test was not the Keystone Algebra I exam. Tutoring was about 40 minutes a day, not a full hour. The general tutoring meta-analysis supports math gains but found larger effects in earlier grades.
